summary.text: Counting multiples of each power \(p^i\) in the gcd product and using the factorial valuation formula gives \(v_p(a(n))=\sum_{i\ge1}\delta(\lfloor n/p^i\rfloor)\), where \(\delta(m)=m^2-\sum_{k=1}^m k\lfloor m/k\rfloor\). Each summand is nonnegative, and direct evaluation for \(m<3\) together with a strict deficit at \(k=m-1\) for \(m\ge3\) shows \(\delta(m)>0\iff m\ge3\); hence the valuation is positive exactly when \(\lfloor n/p\rfloor\ge3\), equivalently \(p\le\lfloor n/3\rfloor\).

full_proof.text:
Let
\[
N(n)=\prod_{j=1}^n\prod_{k=1}^n \gcd(j,k),
\qquad
D(n)=\prod_{k=1}^n\left(\left\lfloor\frac nk\right\rfloor!\right)^k.
\]
Thus the sequence in the statement is
\[
a(n)=\frac{N(n)}{D(n)},
\]
where we will first prove that the division is exact.

For a prime \(p\), write \(v_p(x)\) for the exponent of \(p\) in a positive integer \(x\). We compute the \(p\)-adic valuations of \(N(n)\) and \(D(n)\).

First consider the numerator. For positive \(j,k\),
\[
v_p(\gcd(j,k))=\min(v_p(j),v_p(k)).
\]
Moreover,
\[
\min(v_p(j),v_p(k))
 =\sum_{i\ge 1}\mathbf 1_{p^i\mid j\,\text{ and }\,p^i\mid k}.
\]
Only finitely many terms can be nonzero. Since \(j,k\le n\), it is enough to take \(1\le i\le n\): if \(i>n\), then \(p^i>n\) because \(p\ge2\), so \(p^i\) divides no positive integer at most \(n\). Therefore, after summing over \(j\) and \(k\) and interchanging the finite sums,
\[
\begin{aligned}
v_p(N(n))
&=\sum_{j=1}^n\sum_{k=1}^n
  \min(v_p(j),v_p(k))\\
&=\sum_{i=1}^n
 \#\{j\le n:p^i\mid j\}\,
 \#\{k\le n:p^i\mid k\}.
\end{aligned}
\]
The number of multiples of \(p^i\) among \(1,\dots,n\) is \(\lfloor n/p^i\rfloor\). Hence
\[
\boxed{
 v_p(N(n))=\sum_{i=1}^n
 \left\lfloor\frac{n}{p^i}\right\rfloor^2.}
\tag{1}
\]

We next compute the denominator valuation. By additivity of valuations on products and the rule \(v_p(x^k)=k v_p(x)\),
\[
v_p(D(n))
 =\sum_{k=1}^n k\,v_p\!\left(\left\lfloor\frac nk\right\rfloor!\right).
\]
Legendre’s formula gives, for every nonnegative integer \(r\),
\[
v_p(r!)=\sum_{i\ge1}\left\lfloor\frac{r}{p^i}\right\rfloor.
\]
Again, in the present situation all terms with \(i>n\) vanish, so
\[
\begin{aligned}
v_p(D(n))
&=\sum_{k=1}^n k\sum_{i=1}^n
 \left\lfloor\frac{\lfloor n/k\rfloor}{p^i}\right\rfloor\\
&=\sum_{i=1}^n\sum_{k=1}^n k
 \left\lfloor\frac{n}{k p^i}\right\rfloor.
\end{aligned}
\]
For integer division, successive division satisfies
\[
\left\lfloor\frac{\lfloor n/k\rfloor}{p^i}\right\rfloor
=\left\lfloor\frac{n}{k p^i}\right\rfloor
=\left\lfloor
 \frac{\lfloor n/p^i\rfloor}{k}
 \right\rfloor.
\]
Consequently,
\[
\boxed{
 v_p(D(n))=\sum_{i=1}^n\sum_{k=1}^n
 k\left\lfloor
 \frac{\lfloor n/p^i\rfloor}{k}
 \right\rfloor.}
\tag{2}
\]

We now isolate the difference between (1) and (2). For a nonnegative integer \(m\), define
\[
S(m)=\sum_{k=1}^m k\left\lfloor\frac mk\right\rfloor,
\qquad
\delta(m)=m^2-S(m).
\tag{3}
\]
For each \(1\le k\le m\),
\[
k\left\lfloor\frac mk\right\rfloor\le m.
\]
There are \(m\) terms, and thus
\[
S(m)\le m^2.
\tag{4}
\]
In particular, \(\delta(m)\) is a nonnegative integer.

If \(m\le n\), extending the sum defining \(S(m)\) from \(k\le m\) to \(k\le n\) does not change it, since \(\lfloor m/k\rfloor=0\) for \(k>m\). Thus
\[
\sum_{k=1}^n k\left\lfloor\frac mk\right\rfloor=S(m)
\qquad(m\le n).
\tag{5}
\]
For every \(i\ge1\), the integer
\[
m_i=\left\lfloor\frac{n}{p^i}\right\rfloor
\]
satisfies \(m_i\le n\). Applying (4) and (5), term by term in (1) and (2), gives
\[
\sum_{k=1}^n k\left\lfloor\frac{m_i}{k}\right\rfloor
=S(m_i)\le m_i^2.
\]
It follows that
\[
v_p(D(n))\le v_p(N(n))
\]
for every prime \(p\). Since both \(N(n)\) and \(D(n)\) are positive integers, the prime-factorization criterion for divisibility now yields
\[
D(n)\mid N(n).
\]
This proves in particular that the displayed quotient defining \(a(n)\) is an exact positive integer.

Because the division is exact, subtracting the two valuation formulas is legitimate. Using (3) and (5), we obtain the central formula
\[
\begin{aligned}
v_p(a(n))
&=v_p(N(n))-v_p(D(n))\\
&=\sum_{i=1}^n
\left(
 m_i^2-\sum_{k=1}^n k\left\lfloor\frac{m_i}{k}\right\rfloor
\right)\\
&=\sum_{i=1}^n\delta(m_i).
\end{aligned}
\]
That is,
\[
\boxed{
 v_p(a(n))=
 \sum_{i=1}^n
 \delta\!\left(\left\lfloor\frac{n}{p^i}\right\rfloor\right).}
\tag{6}
\]

It remains to determine exactly when a summand in (6) is positive. We claim that
\[
\boxed{\delta(m)>0\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad m\ge3.}
\tag{7}
\]
For \(m=0,1,2\), this is checked directly:
\[
S(0)=0,
\qquad
S(1)=1,
\qquad
S(2)=1\cdot2+2\cdot1=4.
\]
Thus \(S(m)=m^2\), and hence \(\delta(m)=0\), in all three cases.

Now suppose \(m\ge3\). As observed above, every term in \(S(m)\) is at most \(m\). For the particular index \(k=m-1\), we have
\[
\left\lfloor\frac{m}{m-1}\right\rfloor=1,
\]
because \(m-1\le m<2(m-1)\) when \(m\ge3\). Therefore the corresponding term equals
\[
(m-1)\left\lfloor\frac{m}{m-1}\right\rfloor=m-1<m.
\]
Thus, among the \(m\) terms in \(S(m)\), every term is at most \(m\) and at least one is strictly smaller than \(m\). Hence
\[
S(m)<m\cdot m=m^2,
\]
so \(\delta(m)>0\). This proves (7).

Since all summands in (6) are nonnegative, the sum is positive exactly when at least one summand is positive. By (7),
\[
\begin{aligned}
v_p(a(n))>0
&\Longleftrightarrow
\text{there is some }i\in\{1,\dots,n\}
\text{ such that }
\left\lfloor\frac{n}{p^i}\right\rfloor\ge3.
\end{aligned}
\tag{8}
\]
We show that this condition is equivalent to \(p\le\lfloor n/3\rfloor\).

Suppose first that an index \(i\ge1\) as in (8) exists. Then
\[
3p^i\le n.
\]
Because \(i\ge1\) and \(p\ge2\), we have \(p\le p^i\), and therefore
\[
3p\le3p^i\le n.
\]
Equivalently,
\[
p\le\left\lfloor\frac n3\right\rfloor.
\tag{9}
\]

Conversely, suppose
\[
p\le\left\lfloor\frac n3\right\rfloor.
\]
Then \(3p\le n\), and hence
\[
\left\lfloor\frac np\right\rfloor\ge3.
\]
Taking \(i=1\) in (8) therefore gives a positive summand. Notice that \(3p\le n\) and \(p\ge2\) imply \(n\ge6\), so the index \(i=1\) certainly belongs to \(\{1,\dots,n\}\). Thus \(v_p(a(n))>0\).

Finally, because \(a(n)>0\) and \(p\) is prime,
\[
p\mid a(n)\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad v_p(a(n))>0.
\]
Combining this with (8) and (9) proves, for every positive integer \(n\) and every prime \(p\),
\[
\boxed{
 p\mid a(n)
 \quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
 p\le\left\lfloor\frac n3\right\rfloor.}
\]
